### A. Overview

As illustrated in Fig. 1 and detailed in Fig. 2, RadioTrace embeds the RM-generation and Tx-coordinate-refinement loop into a reverse diffusion process. Starting from a Gaussian initialization  $ \boldsymbol{x}_T \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}) $, the method proceeds through  $ T $ denoising steps. At each reverse step  $ t $, RadioTrace alternates between two steps:

• RM Generation Step: Given the current state  $ \boldsymbol{x}_t $, the iteration index  $ t $, and a binary Tx map  $ C_t $, the fixed generator produces a clean estimate  $ \hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_0^t $ and the denoised RM  $ \boldsymbol{x}_{t-1} $ for the next step  $ t-1 $.
- Tx Update Step: The Tx locations are updated via gradient descent to minimize the reconstruction error between  $ \hat{x}_{0}^{t} $ and the observation O.

By repeating the two steps throughout the reverse diffusion process, RadioTrace progressively recovers both the RM and the Tx locations. In the following subsections, we will explain these two steps in detail.
### B. RM Generation Step

At reverse step $t$, the RM generation step takes the noisy state $\mathbf{x}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{w \times h}$, the building map $B$ and the binary Tx map $C_t \in \{0, 1\}^{w \times h}$ (where $C_t(m, n) = 1$ if and only if a Tx is present at $(m, n)$), and invokes a measurement-free RM generator (diffusion prior) $f_\theta$ whose parameters are trained offline and remain fixed throughout RadioTrace. The generator inputs $(\mathbf{x}_t, t, C_t)$, produces a clean estimate $\mathbf{x}_0^t$, and parameterizes the conditional distribution of $\mathbf{x}_{t-1}$, from which we sample to continue the reverse trajectory. In this step, $C_t$ is treated as a given conditioning signal and its representation and subsequent refinement are deferred to Section III-C.

As illustrated in Fig. 3, the black arrows depict the reverse sampling path used at inference. Operationally, this step performs a single reverse-diffusion update conditioned on  $ (\boldsymbol{x}_{t}, t, \boldsymbol{C}_{t}) $. The generator predicts the injected noise  $ \epsilon_{\theta} $ and yields

$$ \hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{0}^{t}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\Big(\boldsymbol{x}_{t}-\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_{t},t,\boldsymbol{B},\boldsymbol{C}_{t})\Big), $$
$ x_T \longrightarrow \cdots \longrightarrow x_t \xrightarrow{p_\theta(x_{t-1}|x_t, B, C)} x_{t-1} \longrightarrow \cdots \longrightarrow x_0 $ $ q(x_t|x_{t-1}) $

where  $ \bar{\alpha}_{t} = \prod_{i=1}^{t} \alpha_{i} $ follows a fixed noise schedule. The mean of the next noisy state is
$$ \mu_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1})=\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_{t}}(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t-1})\boldsymbol{x}_{t}+(1-\alpha_{t})\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{0}^{t}}{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}, $$
and we draw

$$ \boldsymbol{x}_{t-1}\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\boldsymbol{x}_{t},\boldsymbol{B},\boldsymbol{C}_{t})=\mathcal{N}\big(\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1};\mu_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1}),\gamma_{t}\boldsymbol{I}\big), $$

with variance  $ \gamma_t = \frac{(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t-1})(1-\alpha_t)}{1-\bar{\alpha}_t} $. And the next step noisy RM  $ \boldsymbol{x}_{t-1} $ can be sampled from  $ p_\theta(\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1}|\boldsymbol{x}_t, \boldsymbol{C}_t) $.

Remark. The RM generation step relies on a pre-trained diffusion model  $ f_{\theta} $. There are various ways to obtain such a model. For instance, one may pre-train  $ f_{\theta} $ offline through a measurement-free RM generation task, as in RadioDiff [9]. Our framework primarily focuses on how to leverage this pre-trained model.
### C. Tx Update Step

The measurement-free diffusion prior employed in the RM generation stage can produce accurate radio maps when provided with a precise binary Tx map  $ C_t $. However, in RM estimation,  $ C_t $ is unknown. A straightforward approach is therefore to recover  $ C_t $ from the sampled RSS by minimizing the masked reconstruction error:
$$ \min_{C_{t}\in\{0,1\}^{w\times h}}\left\|\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{0}^{t}(\boldsymbol{C}_{t})\odot\boldsymbol{\mathcal{M}}-\boldsymbol{O}\right\|_{F}^{2}, $$

where  $ \|\cdot\|_{F} $ is the Frobenius norm. However, since  $ C_t $ is high-dimensional and discrete, direct optimization is challenging.
